title: Clergy Act
summary: Ordained ministers and Christian Science practitioners can apply to permanently opt out of Social Security and Medicare taxes on their ministerial earnings — but that exemption is currently irrevocable. This bill creates a one-time window for those who previously opted out to reverse that decision and re-enter the Social Security system, with coverage beginning for taxable years starting after December 31, 2027. Once revoked, they cannot opt out again.
brief: Creates a one-time window for clergy who opted out of Social Security to reverse that decision and begin accruing retirement benefits.

top_lines.headline: One-Time Re-entry Window
subs: Clergy may revoke their Social Security exemption by filing through the deadline for their second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2027
Coverage begins for taxable years starting after December 31, 2027 — cannot opt out again after revoking

top_lines.headline: IRS Outreach Required
subs: Commissioner of Internal Revenue must submit a plan to inform eligible clergy of their eligibility within 90 days of enactment

likelihoodReason: The bill has 21 cosponsors and bipartisan backing — sponsors include Fong (R-CA), Thompson (D-CA), and Kelly (R-PA). Providing clergy a window to undo a permanent decision is unlikely to draw opposition. The narrow scope and sympathetic affected population make Senate passage plausible, though floor scheduling is uncertain.

items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Revocation of Social Security Exemption

items.main: Notwithstanding Section 1402(e)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code (which makes the Social Security exemption irrevocable), clergy whose exemption is in effect for the taxable year of enactment may revoke it by filing an application with the IRS.
items.detail: The application must be filed no later than the due date for the second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2027. Revocation takes effect for the first or second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2027, as specified by the applicant, and covers both chapter 2 of the IRC (self-employment tax) and title II of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 401 et seq.). If the application is filed retroactively for a year already in effect, the applicant must pay in full all self-employment taxes that would have been owed for that year. After revoking, the applicant may not again file for an exemption under Section 1402(e)(1).

items.main: The Commissioner of Internal Revenue, in consultation with the Commissioner of Social Security, must develop and submit a plan to inform eligible clergy of their revocation eligibility within 90 days of enactment.
items.detail: The plan must be submitted to the Ways and Means Committee of the House and the Finance Committee of the Senate. No minimum outreach activities, funding level, or success metrics are specified in the bill.

underreported.summary: If a clergy member files a revocation application after the due date for a taxable year and elects to have it take effect for that year, they must immediately pay all self-employment taxes that would have been owed for the entire year.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's headline is a window to opt back in. The catch-up payment requirement means that choosing early retroactive coverage triggers a lump-sum tax obligation for the full year of retroactive coverage — a condition not apparent from the bill's title or the primary revocation provision.

criticisms.why: Mr. Speaker, if we are serious about strengthening Social Security, we can't stop at incremental fixes. We must also protect the program from efforts that would weaken this great program. We have heard calls for so-called reforms or tough choices. Let's be clear about what that means: cutting benefits, raising retirement age, or moving toward privatization--steps that undermine the guaranteed security Americans rely on. Democrats reject that approach. We believe Social Security is a promise, not a bargaining chip.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fong
featured_quotes.text: This bipartisan legislation, cosponsored by my fellow California Congressman Mike Thompson, would create a one-time re- enrollment window for pastors and other clergy members who have previously opted out of Social Security, many in their youth, to voluntarily opt back in. For decades, members of the clergy have made the permanent decision of opting out of Social Security. While this choice was made with good intentions, many faith leaders experience significant financial hardship as they approach retirement.

gaps: The bill allows revocation effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2027 but does not address Social Security credits for prior years during which the exemption was in effect — those years generate no credits regardless of revocation.
The 90-day outreach plan requirement specifies no minimum outreach activities, distribution channels, or funding, leaving the scope of IRS notification entirely to agency discretion.
